In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the presence of two copies of all these elements is required for efficient DNA supercoiling by gyrase.
the two-fold symmetry of gyrase is required for the supercoiled DNA product, but that it is not necessary for the individual steps of the reaction.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the two CTD domains of gyrase play different roles in the negative supercoiling reaction of DNA: One CTD is involved in the stabilization of the positive DNA node and thus in the supercoiling step, whereas the other CTD is required for the strand passage step.
the two CTD domains are not redundant in the sense that they can be exchanged without any loss of function.
the two-fold symmetry of gyrase has evolved to enable the enzyme to supercoil DNA more efficiently.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the two-fold symmetry of gyrase is essential to its function, and that the two-fold symmetric structure of gyrase has evolved for the purpose of supercoiling DNA.
, while the CTDs are not required for DNA cleavage, ATP hydrolysis and strand passage, they do stabilize the positive node, and thus facilitate the transition from a positive to a negative DNA node.
the two-fold symmetry of gyrase allows for a more efficient reaction than a monomeric enzyme.
